## Overview

Most of my youth and current years on the internet has been spent on Tumblr, where it has a unique case of being a platform where a big chunk of the user base actively resists being recommended to. Which is why I decided to analyze its current recommender system, to learn more on their user base and possible rooms of improvements for this assignment.


## Scenario Design #1: Tumblr (the Organization)

In July 2023, Tumblr staff posted a "Core Product Strategy" that explained the problem from the company's side: Tumblr had historically expected users to curate their own feeds, but that adds friction and only works for a small slice of its audience ([Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/tumblrs-building-a-tiktok-inspired-feed-in-bid-to-grow-its-user-base-220929704.html)).

The users' side went very differently. A lot of the existing user base protested, especially at the idea that an algorithmic feed could replace the classic chronological one. The most viral poll got over 130,000 votes in a single day and showed overwhelming opposition ([Know Your Meme](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/events/2023-tumblr-changes)).


**1. Who are the target users?**

This is Tumblr's product team, working inside Automattic.

The team is small and under pressure. A leaked 2023 memo from CEO Matt Mullenweg said Automattic hadn't gotten the results it expected from the 600+ person-years of effort put into Tumblr since the acquisition ([Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Tumblr)). Starting in 2024, Tumblr moved to smaller, more focused teams working on the core parts of the site ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2023/11/09/tumblr-to-run-on-skeleton-crew-as-parent-company-automattic-absorbs-staff)).

**2. What are their key goals?**

- Grow the user base and keep new users around.
- Help creators reach audiences.
- Eventually make the platform sustainable, since Tumblr still isn't profitable.

The 2023 strategy laid out six guiding principles:

1.  Expand how new users discover Tumblr and sign up
2.  Show high-quality content when users open the app
3.  Make conversations easier to participate in
4.  Retain and grow creators
5.  Give users more reasons to return
6.  Improve performance, stability, and overall quality

**3. How can the recommender help them accomplish those goals?**

- **Better ranking.** Tumblr said it wanted to "improve our algorithmic ranking capabilities across all feeds."
- **Solving cold start for newbies.** A brand-new user follows nobody, so a purely follow-based dashboard is empty. Recommendations fill that gap.
- **Reach for smaller creators.** Recommendations can push newer or smaller creators to people outside their own follower networks.

### Scenario Design #2: Tumblr's Users

Tumblr's users aren't one group, so I split them into three.

**1. Who are the target users?**

- **Longtime users.** They built their dashboard by hand over years and are deeply attached to it.
- **New users.** Many are Gen Z, and they often show up from other platforms during moments of chaos. For example, sign-ups jumped as the US TikTok ban got close, and again when Brazil temporarily banned X ([Android Headlines](https://www.androidheadlines.com/2025/04/tumblr-is-reportedly-reviving-as-gen-z-take-interest-in-the-platform.html)).
- **Creators.** Artists, writers, fan creators, and meme-makers. Tumblr is famously where fandoms form around shared interests.

\[Add a line here about which group *you* fall into and how you use Tumblr.\]

**2. What are their key goals?**

- **Longtime users want control and chronology.** Many say that being able to curate their own experience, without an algorithm deciding for them, is the main reason they use Tumblr at all.
- **New users want to find their people fast.** They're looking for their fandom or niche without needing a PhD in Tumblr culture first.
- **Creators want their work seen** by the right audience, without being forced to chase engagement.
- **Everyone wants to avoid content they don't want to see**, whether that's spoilers, triggering topics, or mature content.

**3. How can the recommender help them accomplish those goals?**

- **Let users choose how much algorithm they get.** Turning off "Include posts liked by the blogs you follow," "Best stuff first," and "Based on your likes" leaves only posts from blogs you follow, newest first.
- **Organize discovery around interests, not virality.** Communities give users dedicated feeds separate from the algorithmic "For You" and chronological "Following" feeds. They can be as broad as Taylor Swift fans or as niche as fans of the *Wicked* book who haven't seen the musical ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2024/05/28/tumblr-launches-its-semi-private-communities-in-open-beta)).
- **Let users filter.** Community labels let posts be tagged for drug and alcohol addiction, violence, and sexual content, and users under 18 are automatically blocked from seeing labeled content ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2022/09/27/tumblr-bring-back-porn-nsfw-community-labels)).

## Reverse Engineering Tumblr's Recommender

Tumblr hasn't published a detailed paper on its recommender models the way Amazon or the NYT did, so part of this is educated guessing. But there's more public info than you'd expect, mostly because Tumblr open-sourced part of its stack.

### What I Can See in the Interface

\[Screenshot: Dashboard settings page\]

\[Screenshot: For You and Following tabs\]

Here's every recommendation "surface" I could find:

- **Following feed.** Posts from blogs you follow. It's chronological by default, and becomes ranked if "Best stuff first" is on.
- **Best Stuff First.** Pushes what Tumblr considers the best posts from blogs you follow, apparently based mostly on note count, to the top of your dashboard. That's a popularity ranking applied to your own network.
- **Stuff in Your Orbit.** Shows posts liked by people you follow.
- **Based on Your Likes.** Recommended posts based on what you've liked.
- **Followed tags.** Posts from tags you follow, mixed into your dashboard.
- **For You, Explore/Trending, Communities, and tag search pages.**
- **Onboarding.** A new account's dashboard is full of recommendations based on the topics picked during sign-up, and you see fewer as you follow more blogs.

\[Add anything else you notice in your own account, like recommended blogs or Blaze (paid promotion) posts.\]

### Under the Hood: StreamBuilder

This was the coolest find. Tumblr open-sourced the framework behind its feeds. It's called **StreamBuilder**, it's written in PHP (a language I work in, so I can actually read it), and the code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/Automattic/stream-builder). According to Tumblr's announcement:

- It powers the Following feed, For You, search results, blog pages, tag pages, and blog recommendations.
- Posts from blogs you follow, posts from tags you follow, and blog recommendations are each a **separate stream** with its own logic, all built on the same framework.
- Recommendations are **injected at set intervals**, posts are **filtered** based on who you've blocked, and posts are **ranked for relevance** only if "Best stuff first" is turned on.

Based on that, here's my best guess at how a dashboard gets built:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Followed blogs stream] --> D[Mix streams]
    B[Followed tags stream] --> D
    C[Recommendation streams<br/>Based on likes / Orbit] --> E[Inject at intervals]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Filter<br/>blocks, filtered tags,<br/>community labels]
    F --> G{Best stuff first?}
    G -- on --> H[Rank by engagement]
    G -- off --> I[Sort chronologically]
    H --> J[Dashboard]
    I --> J
```

### Mapping It to Chapter 9

| Chapter 9 concept | How I think it shows up on Tumblr |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Utility matrix** | Users × posts, filled with *implicit* feedback (likes, reblogs, replies, follows) instead of star ratings. It's basically 1s and blanks, and a blank doesn't mean "disliked." |
| **Content-based filtering** | **Tags are the item profiles.** The chapter literally discusses tags as a way to get item features, and Tumblr is built on them. The topics you pick at sign-up act as your starting user profile. |
| **Collaborative filtering** | "Based on Your Likes" looks like item-item or user-user collaborative filtering. "Stuff in Your Orbit" is a *social* version, where your "similar users" are just the people you follow. |
| **Popularity / engagement** | Best Stuff First and Trending rank by notes. Exactly how Tumblr weighs likes vs. reblogs vs. replies isn't public, but likes clearly matter since there's a whole feature built on them. |
| **Hybrid / blending** | StreamBuilder mixes several independent streams into one feed, which is the same "combine multiple models" lesson from the Netflix Prize. |
| **Jaccard vs. cosine** | Since the data is mostly 1s and blanks, Jaccard-style similarity over likes, follows, or tags would make sense. (My guess, not confirmed.) |

**My overall take:** Tumblr's recommender is a lightweight hybrid. It leans on user-curated signals (follows, tags), adds popularity ranking and collaborative-style recommendations as optional layers, and wraps everything in a lot of user toggles. It's more "recommendation as a side dish" than TikTok's "recommendation is the whole meal."

### Context That Affects What's Possible

- **Small team.** After missing its 2023 growth goals, Tumblr refocused on core functionality with a smaller staff.
- **Backend migration on hold.** In 2025, Automattic paused moving Tumblr's backend to WordPress, with Mullenweg saying the focus would shift to what users actually ask for ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/01/automattic-puts-tumblr-migration-to-wordpress-on-hold/)).

In other words, any improvement has to be realistic for a small team.

## Recommendations for Improving Tumblr's Recommender

1.  **Ship "Collections" to fix onboarding.** Tumblr Labs already floated the idea of followable collections of blogs and tags, curated around interests and moods. User-made "starter packs" (like "Broadway Tumblr 101") would solve cold start with *human* curation, which fits the culture way better than forcing an algorithmic feed on people.

2.  **Add a "Why am I seeing this?" label to every injected post.** StreamBuilder already knows which stream each post came from (followed tag, Orbit, Based on Your Likes), so showing that should be cheap. Transparency builds trust with a user base that's suspicious of algorithms.


3.  **Let users pick (or build) their own algorithm.** Mullenweg has said he imagines users choosing their own algorithm ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2023/08/23/automattic-ceo-matt-mullenweg-talks-future-of-tumblr-with-algorithmic-choice-ai-enhancements-and-more)). Since StreamBuilder is open source, Tumblr could let users choose from community-made feeds (like "reblogs with commentary only" or "small creators first"), similar to Bluesky's custom feeds.

4.  **Fix popularity bias for small creators.** Ranking by raw note count rewards whatever's already viral (the long-tail problem from Chapter 9). Two specific fixes:

    - Weight reblogs that add commentary or tags more heavily than bare likes.
    - Add time decay, since old posts often recirculate on Tumblr for years.

5.  **Treat accessibility as a recommendation feature.** Tumblr has a strong culture of image descriptions. Posts with alt text or image IDs could be tagged as a content feature, and users could get a toggle to prioritize described posts. As someone who works on WCAG compliance, I think this would help disabled users find content they can actually use, and reward creators who make their posts accessible.

6.  **Measure success beyond engagement.** Learn from Netflix: the "most accurate" algorithm isn't automatically the right one. Tumblr should track how many new users stick around, how often people turn recommendation toggles *off*, and user satisfaction surveys, not just time-on-site.

## Conclusion

Doing scenario design twice showed me the core tension:

- **Tumblr the company** needs recommendations to grow and survive.
- **Tumblr's users** chose the platform partly *because* it doesn't shove an algorithm in their face.

The best path forward isn't picking a side. It's building recommendations that are **opt-in, transparent, interest-driven, and community-curated**. Tumblr's open-source StreamBuilder and its culture of tags and Communities already give it the building blocks. It just needs to lean into what makes it different instead of trying to become TikTok.
